To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
GHG emissions have been stabilised, mainly due to the decrease in the carbon intensity of the economy.

In the period 2001-2008, the increase in the Greek GHG emissions was 1.6%, mainly attributed to the increase in population (+1.3%) and economic growth (+0.3%) and to the increase in the carbon intensity of the energy mix (+0.1%).
GHG emissions have increased slightly in 2008, compared to 2007, and have almost stabilised since 2000.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying the factors that have contributed to the stabilisation of GHG emissions in Greece over the last eight years.
the analysis of the relationship between the main drivers and pressures of climate change.
the identification of the main drivers of GHG emissions in Greece and their interrelations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the GHG emissions of Greece have stabilised over the period 1990-2008.
the GHG emissions of Greece are not increasing and the drivers of climate change are not affecting the GHG emissions.
the GHG emissions in Greece are stabilised, but they are expected to increase in the near future.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GHG emissions have not increased in the last years in Greece.
the energy intensity and carbon intensity are the main factors affecting GHG emissions, while GDP has a secondary role.
Greece is a country with a high energy intensity of GDP, a high carbon intensity of energy consumption and high GHG intensity of population.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the energy intensity and the carbon intensity are the two main factors affecting the GHG emissions in Greece.
the drivers of pressures are not independent, but rather they interact in a complex way, which makes it difficult to predict future trends of GHG emissions.
the drivers of pressures are the key to understanding the trends and patterns of emissions.
